title: Monadic IO
body:
How a language with no side effects reads a file. The answer is not an exception to
[[Pure Function|purity]] and this is the thing to get right: **an `IO a` is a description of an
action, not the action.** Building one is pure and does nothing. The runtime performs the
description that `main` finally evaluates to.

```haskell
greet :: IO ()
greet = do
    putStrLn "Name?"          -- a value of type IO (), not a print that happened
    name <- getLine           -- getLine :: IO String; name :: String
    putStrLn ("Hi " ++ name)

main :: IO ()
main = greet                  -- the runtime runs this one
```

`putStrLn "Name?"` on its own, in the middle of a pure function, prints nothing. It is a value
you can put in a list, pass to a function, or throw away, the same as `5` or `"hello"`. The
usual mental model is that an `IO a` is a recipe, and `main` is the only recipe anyone cooks.

## Why this preserves purity

Every function above is still a [[Pure Function]] by the two-clause definition: same input,
same output, nothing else changed. `greet` is a *constant*, a fixed description, evaluated the
same way every time. The effects happen outside the language, performed by the runtime on the
value the program produced.

The type is also a wall. There is no function `IO a -> a`, so an effect cannot leak into pure
code: a function whose type is `Int -> Int` **cannot** have read a file, because it had no `IO`
to get the value out of. This is the strongest thing the type system says in the whole course,
and it is why [[Static Typing]] and purity are the same design decision. Effects are visible in
the signature, always, and there is no way to hide one.

The cost is real: the wall is one-directional and it propagates. Add logging to a function deep
in a pure call tree and every caller's type changes from `a -> b` to `a -> IO b`, all the way
up. That is honest bookkeeping (the change *is* a change in what those functions do) and it is
also genuinely annoying, and it is the standard complaint against the design.

## Where the [[Monad]] comes in

Two effects must happen in order, and `name <- getLine` needs the *value* of the read to build
the next action. That is precisely what `>>=` provides, so `IO` is a [[Monad]] and the `do`
block desugars like any other:

```haskell
getLine >>= \name -> putStrLn ("Hi " ++ name)
```

The monad gives sequencing for free. The lambda cannot run before `getLine` produces a value, so
the data dependency *is* the ordering, and no special "statement" concept is needed in a
language whose evaluation order is otherwise unspecified ([[Lazy Evaluation]]). That is the neat
part: `>>=` is how a lazy language recovers a defined order exactly where it needs one and
nowhere else.

## Against the alternative

| Language | Where effects may occur | How you know |
|---|---|---|
| [[C]], [[Java]], [[JavaScript]] | anywhere | you read the body, and the bodies it calls |
| [[Haskell]] | only in `IO` | the type says so |

The [[Void]] note (COMP 3612) describes a function that exists only for its side effect. In
Haskell that function's type is `IO ()`, and the `()` is doing the same job `void` does while
the `IO` adds the part C leaves out: *which* function is allowed to.

## Core Facts to Know

- An `IO a` is a **description** of an effect, a value, not a performed action.
- Building it is pure; only the runtime, evaluating `main`, performs it.
- Therefore purity is not violated: effect-free functions stay effect-free.
- There is no `IO a -> a`, so effects cannot leak into pure code.
- A signature without `IO` is a guarantee the function did no input or output.
- The cost: adding an effect deep in a call tree changes every caller's type.
- `IO` is a [[Monad]]; `>>=` supplies the ordering a [[Lazy Evaluation|lazy]] language lacks.
- The data dependency in `x <- action` is what forces the sequencing.
- `main :: IO ()` is the one action the runtime executes.
